summary:
Guadeloupe is a French overseas department and an integral part of France rather than a separate jurisdiction. French national law applies in full, covering criminal provisions, identity documents, detention and the national protection bodies, and the island has no legislation of its own in these areas; that framework is carried by the France record, and this assessment covers only what is specific to the island.

The island's first LGBT+ centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024, providing reception, support and orientation for people of diverse sexual, gender and bodily identities.

Government minister Aurore Bergé attended the opening and announced measures to strengthen the response to gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, including structures adapted to the overseas departments.

Local groups Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova planned a year of social events across Guadeloupe in 2025.
tangentialFactors:
Because these matters are set nationally, changes in French law take effect in Guadeloupe without a separate local vote, and the island has no regional legislature to modify or delay them.

Activism in Guadeloupe is described as having advanced later than in Martinique.
localsOnly:
The Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion is run by a federation of Guadeloupean associations and serves residents of the island, offering reception, support and orientation for people of diverse sexual, gender and bodily identities.

Local accounts describe community members increasingly reconciling their lives with their orientation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Guadeloupe-specific data on anti-trans violence, policing practice, healthcare access or facilities was identified in the sources reviewed. National-level statistics and detention findings are carried by the France record.

The funding arrangements of the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion and the implementation of the measures announced at its opening are not documented in the sources.
